profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a developer tools company about an internal proposal for an ML-assisted code review feature called 'ReviewAid'. The proposal describes a first production pilot that ranks incoming pull request comments by likely usefulness and suggests missing review comments to human reviewers. The team has already aligned on the broad product direction, and this meeting is to review whether the design is ready for pilot approval. The context is that the proposal was written after surveying prior automated code review research and explicitly tries to avoid known evaluation pitfalls such as temporal leakage and inconsistent task definitions. The agenda is to review the proposed offline evaluation plan, artifact packaging for reproducibility, and what counts as 'pilot-ready' for the design. The expected outcome is a decision on whether the design can move forward with minor edits or needs another revision round.

members.name: Lena Park
members.expertise: Applied machine learning for developer tooling, offline evaluation design, ranking systems
members.background: Lena has spent six years building ML features for IDEs and repository analytics platforms and recently led an internal effort to standardize evaluation practices for code intelligence models.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved this week so the team can reserve compute and begin implementation before the next quarterly planning cutoff; she is especially concerned about avoiding obvious methodological criticism while keeping the evaluation process lightweight enough to execute quickly.
hidden_assumptions: If the proposal says the evaluation is 'temporally clean', that means train/dev/test are split by pull request creation month, which is the standard she uses internally.

A 'reproducible package' for design approval means pinned code, feature extraction scripts, and split manifests stored in the internal ML registry; raw review text does not need to be redistributed again if it already exists in the warehouse.

When a design says 'human-level sanity check', a small expert spot-check on around 200 sampled comments is sufficient because the pilot gate is about catching glaring failures, not producing publishable annotation evidence.
For a pilot design review, fairness and multilingual behavior are noted risks but remain outside scope unless they block the core English-language repository rollout.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.role: Principal Software Engineer, Code Review Platform
members.expertise: Code review infrastructure, repository lifecycle data, production rollout readiness
members.background: Arjun has worked on the company's pull request and review systems for nearly a decade and often represents platform reliability and operational concerns in cross-functional design reviews.
members.private_state: He wants to support the ML initiative but is quietly trying to ensure the pilot does not create downstream operational churn for the review platform or force his team to clean up an under-specified dataset and release process later.
hidden_assumptions: If the proposal says the evaluation is 'temporally clean', that means every feature used at scoring time must have been available before the first review comment on that pull request, not merely that examples are split by month.

A 'reproducible package' means another engineer outside the originating team can rebuild the benchmark end to end, including the exact review snapshots and text normalization steps, without depending on mutable warehouse tables.
A 'human-level sanity check' means at least a structured side-by-side review by multiple reviewers with disagreement resolution, because otherwise low-quality suggestions will slip into the pilot.
If the design is called 'pilot-ready', it includes integration-boundary clarifications like which repositories, languages, and moderation flows are in scope, even if the model design itself is fixed.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as a temporally clean split
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both endorse using a 'temporally clean' evaluation split.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means data is partitioned by pull request creation month so later pull requests do not appear in training.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means no feature or label signal from after review start can influence scoring, including metadata that stabilizes only after the full review thread exists.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both are sophisticated and strongly agree that temporal bias matters, so the shared phrase feels precise enough; each assumes the other is using the same well-known notion of temporal cleanliness.

misalignment_points.topic: What the reproducibility artifact must include
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both say the benchmark should be shipped as a 'reproducible package'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes reproducibility is satisfied by checked-in training code, dependency versions, feature schemas, and immutable split IDs pointing to existing internal sources.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes reproducibility requires a self-contained rebuild path with frozen snapshots or exports of the review data and preprocessing outputs so future engineers can reconstruct the benchmark exactly.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML teams, 'reproducible package' is common shorthand and both think they are asking for good engineering hygiene; the disagreement is about the threshold for completeness, not about whether reproducibility matters.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They both discuss whether the design is 'pilot-ready'.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats pilot-ready as meaning the model evaluation and safety checks are adequate for a limited English-only experiment, while repo onboarding details can be finalized during implementation.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats pilot-ready as including enough rollout-boundary detail now to avoid later ambiguity about repository eligibility, unsupported languages, and moderation/escalation behavior.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Design reviews often collapse model readiness and rollout readiness into the same approval conversation, so both can keep using the same phrase while silently evaluating different boundaries.

misalignment_points.topic: What a human sanity check entails
misalignment_points.surface_form: They both agree to add a 'human sanity check' before the pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 plans a fast expert inspection of a few hundred sampled suggestions by one or two internal reviewers to validate obvious plausibility.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 expects a lightweight but formal review exercise with multiple raters, explicit criteria, and adjudication on disagreements before exposing suggestions in the platform.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because both view this as a secondary guardrail rather than the core evaluation, they speak in broad terms and do not spell out the operational procedure.

turns.inner_thought: I want this to land today with only small edits so we can lock compute before quarterly planning closes. The proposal is already strong on the model side, and for me 'pilot-ready' means the offline eval is defensible enough for a limited English-only experiment. We do not need to settle every onboarding and operations detail before approval.

We already folded in the big lessons from the recent automated review work, especially around evaluation pitfalls, so from my side this is mostly about confirming it's pilot-ready with a few tightening edits.

turns.utterance: Yes, that's covered in the way we've set up the benchmark. The split manifests are frozen, the feature pipeline is pinned, and all of that will live in the reproducible package, so we should be in good shape on leakage concerns and it should be easy to rerun later.

turns.inner_thought: Now I should get to the safety guardrail so he feels comfortable approving. For me the human sanity check is a quick expert spot-check on a couple hundred samples to catch glaring nonsense before any pilot exposure. turns.utterance: On the quality side, before anything launches we'll add a human sanity check on sampled suggestions. The goal there is just to make sure obviously bad comments don't make it in front of pilot users, even if the offline numbers look good.

turns.inner_thought: Good, she already expects a human sanity check. turns.inner_thought: That sounds compatible enough and still lightweight.
